title: Banjo in his early band, George Potter and pianist Frankie Frober
summary: Asked about banjo use, DeDroit says his 1917 band had trumpet, clarinet and trombone, then tells how banjoist George Potter and his New York pianist went their ways.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Well, I'll tell you. My wife is a graduate of Newcomb. She's a psychologist and all like that.

One of the great crossword puzzles is the fact that I lived so long that I know some of the words. She never heard of them. These are all right up to bamboo. Now that was a big affair. It didn't look just there to put down. Stop it in a moment. Now this... Hang up again. Didn't you meet her? Yes, I met her, but I didn't know I used to work with her. All right. She's the sweetest. I'll tell you. She spoils me. I'm rotten. When you first started your Dixieland band in 1917, you were using a banjo at that time? No, I was using trumpet, clarinet, trombone.
I see. Were other of the groups that were around using banjos at that time, do you remember?
Well, yes, they were. George was playing at the Absinthe House. That's where I got him.

George Potter. When I left New York, he stayed up there and he went with Tad Teeman. And the piano player I had in New York was named Frankie Frober. A lot of them called him Fraber. He made quite a reputation. They called him a backroom pianist. He used to wear a straw hat and all the daughters. Great piano player. But he was young and he was stricken with appendicitis and Harris Boyd. And so he wanted to stay up in the air. And he said, well, maybe he was greater in New York than he would have been in New York. You know, those things happen, you know? Sure. Is there anything I can ask? I'm taking up your time tonight.
